plan: SAT R&W batch 65: 10 new items on new passages CLD-P-SAT-RW-000582..000591 (Hokusai Prussian blue WIC, okapi inference, fertilizer-by-light quantitative evidence, Wallace/Darwin cross-text, Jacquard and Babbage purpose, Wallace Line possessive, Banneker verb tense, Grace Hopper transition, Rosalind Franklin synthesis, Langston Hughes "Dreams" (1923, public domain) quotation). Topics checked against every bank and the combined bank. Plus S064-09 resubmitted as revision 2 on its previously unbanked passage. Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A new blue
passages.text: Katsushika Hokusai's print The Great Wave off Kanagawa, made around 1831, uses large areas of Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment that had only recently become ______ in Japan: imported by Dutch and Chinese traders, it had once been too costly for most printmakers, but by the late 1820s it was cheap enough for mass-produced woodblock prints.

passages.title: A misleading pattern
passages.text: The okapi, a forest animal of central Africa, was well known to local people but unknown to European zoologists until 1901. The first reports to reach Europe were based on strips of skin with bold horizontal stripes like those of a zebra, and some scientists guessed the animal was a kind of forest zebra. When a complete skin and two skulls were examined, however, the skulls' features closely matched those of giraffes. This history suggests that ______

passages.title: Light and fertilizer
passages.text:
A student grew bean plants with two fertilizers under two light levels and recorded the average height after four weeks.
Low light: fertilizer A 12 cm, fertilizer B 13 cm
High light: fertilizer A 20 cm, fertilizer B 28 cm
The student claims that fertilizer B's advantage over fertilizer A depended strongly on the amount of light.

passages.title: Two discoverers
passages.text:
Text 1
Popular accounts often present the theory of evolution by natural selection as the work of Charles Darwin alone, tracing it to his voyage on HMS Beagle and his book On the Origin of Species, published in 1859.

Text 2
In 1858, the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, working in what is now Indonesia, sent Darwin an essay describing a process of natural selection much like the one Darwin had been developing privately for years. That July, papers by both men were presented together at a meeting of the Linnean Society in London, and Darwin hurried to finish the book he published the next year.

passages.title: Cards that weave
passages.text: In 1804, Joseph-Marie Jacquard patented a loom attachment that used a chain of punched cards to control which threads were raised for each pass of the shuttle, so that complex patterns could be woven automatically. Decades later, Charles Babbage planned to use similar punched cards to feed instructions and numbers into his Analytical Engine, a mechanical calculating machine that he designed but never completed.

passages.title: A line on the map
passages.text: While collecting animals in the Malay Archipelago in the 1850s, Alfred Russel Wallace noticed that the islands' animals fell into two sharply different groups, one Asian and one Australian. The ______ observations of these distributions led him to propose a boundary between the two groups, now called the Wallace Line.

passages.title: A letter with an almanac
passages.text: In 1791, before his first almanac was published, the self-taught astronomer and surveyor Benjamin Banneker ______ a manuscript copy of his calculations to Thomas Jefferson, along with a letter challenging Jefferson's views on race.

passages.title: Words for machines
passages.text: In the early 1950s, many computer scientists assumed that computers could be programmed only in numerical code. Grace Hopper disagreed, and in 1952 she and her team completed a compiler, a program that translated instructions written in a more humanlike notation into machine code. ______ her work helped lead to COBOL, a programming language introduced in 1959 that used English words such as ADD and MOVE.

passages.title: Notes on an image
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In 1952, Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling made an X-ray image of DNA known as Photo 51.
- In 1953, Maurice Wilkins showed the image to James Watson without Franklin's knowledge.
- Watson and Francis Crick published their double-helix model of DNA later in 1953.
- Franklin died in 1958.
- The 1962 Nobel Prize for the structure of DNA went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins.
- Nobel Prizes are not awarded after a person's death.

passages.title: A broken wing
passages.text: "Dreams" is a 1923 poem by Langston Hughes. In the poem, the speaker suggests that life without dreams loses the ability to rise and move freely.

passages.title: Notes on a ship
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- The Clotilda was the last known ship to bring enslaved Africans to the United States, arriving in Alabama in 1860, decades after the trade was outlawed.
- After the voyage, the ship was burned to hide evidence of the crime.
- Many of the people it carried later founded Africatown, a community near Mobile.
- Descendants of those people still live in Africatown.
- In 2019, researchers confirmed that a wreck in the Mobile River was the Clotilda.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: cheap enough for mass-produced woodblock prints
candidates.explanation: A pigment that was once too costly but became cheap enough for mass production had become "affordable."

A.rationale: The pigment was newly in use, not outdated.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the pigment was banned; the issue was cost.

D.rationale: All pigments are decorative; the text's explanation concerns price.

candidates.remember: Let the explanation after the colon define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: local people had wrongly believed the okapi was related to zebras.
choices.B: giraffes once had striped legs like those of the okapi.
choices.C: the striped skin had misled scientists about the okapi's closest relatives.
choices.D: skull features are less reliable than skin patterns for classifying animals.

candidates.evidence: the skulls' features closely matched those of giraffes
candidates.explanation: Early guesses based on striped skin pointed to zebras, but the skulls showed a giraffe relationship, so the stripes had misled the scientists.

A.rationale: The text says local people knew the animal well and does not report their beliefs about its relatives.

B.rationale: The text does not discuss the appearance of ancient giraffes.

D.rationale: The skulls corrected the error that the skin had caused, which suggests the opposite.

hints: What did the skin suggest, and what did the skulls show?

strategy.explanation: Contrast the early guess with the later evidence.

candidates.remember: An inference should explain a contrast the text sets up.

candidates.stem: Which choice best uses data from the text to support the student's claim?

choices.A: Fertilizer B's plants were 8 cm taller than A's in high light but only 1 cm taller in low light.
choices.B: Plants given fertilizer B grew to 28 cm in high light, the greatest average height recorded.
choices.C: Plants given fertilizer A grew 8 cm taller in high light than in low light.
choices.D: Plants given either fertilizer grew taller in high light than in low light.

candidates.evidence: fertilizer B's advantage over fertilizer A depended strongly on the amount of light
candidates.explanation: B's advantage is the difference between B and A: 28 − 20 = 8 cm in high light versus 13 − 12 = 1 cm in low light.

B.rationale: This gives one value but does not compare B's advantage across light levels.

C.rationale: This describes the effect of light on A alone, not B's advantage over A.

D.rationale: This is true but says nothing about whether B's advantage changed.

hints: How do you measure B's advantage?

strategy.explanation: Compute the B − A difference at each light level.

candidates.remember: Support a comparison claim with the compared quantities.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the popular accounts described in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that Wallace, not Darwin, should be credited as the theory's only author
choices.B: By claiming that Darwin borrowed the idea of natural selection from Wallace's essay
choices.C: By agreeing that On the Origin of Species was the first public statement of the theory
choices.D: By noting that they overlook Wallace's independent role in developing the theory

candidates.evidence: papers by both men were presented together
candidates.explanation: Text 2 shows that Wallace arrived at the same idea independently and that both were presented together in 1858, which popular accounts leave out.

A.rationale: Text 2 presents the two as developing the idea independently, not Wallace alone.

B.rationale: Text 2 says Darwin had been developing the idea privately for years.

C.rationale: Text 2 says both men's papers were presented in 1858, before the book.

hints: What does Text 2 add that Text 1 omits?

strategy.explanation: Compare who gets credit in each text.

candidates.remember: Look for what one text says the other leaves out.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To describe an invention and show how its key idea was later adapted
choices.B: To argue that Babbage's machine failed because it depended on Jacquard's design
choices.C: To explain how weavers resisted the introduction of automatic looms
choices.D: To compare the patterns produced by Jacquard's loom with earlier hand weaving

candidates.evidence: planned to use similar punched cards
candidates.explanation: The text describes Jacquard's punched-card loom and then shows Babbage adapting the same punched-card idea for a calculating machine.

B.rationale: The text gives no reason for the machine's incompletion.

C.rationale: The text does not mention weavers' reactions.

D.rationale: The text does not discuss earlier weaving.

hints: How are the two sentences connected?
candidates.remember: A purpose answer should cover the whole text.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: led him to propose a boundary
candidates.explanation: The observations belong to one naturalist, Wallace, so the singular possessive "naturalist's" is correct.

A.rationale: The plural possessive refers to more than one naturalist, but only Wallace is meant.

B.rationale: A plural noun without an apostrophe cannot show possession here.

D.rationale: The singular noun without an apostrophe cannot modify "observations" as an owner.

strategy.explanation: Decide singular or plural, then possessive.

candidates.remember: Singular possessive: add 's to the singular noun.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: In 1791, before his first almanac was published
candidates.explanation: The sentence describes a completed action in 1791, so the simple past "sent" is correct.

A.rationale: The present tense does not fit an event in 1791.

C.rationale: The present perfect does not fit an action completed at a specific past time.

D.rationale: The future tense does not fit a past event.

candidates.remember: Use the simple past for a completed action at a stated past time.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.explanation: The text moves from 1952 to a language introduced in 1959 that grew out of her work, so a time transition fits.

B.rationale: COBOL's creation is not an example of the 1952 compiler.

C.rationale: COBOL built on her compiler rather than replacing it.

D.rationale: Nothing in the text works against the development of COBOL.

hints: How are the two events related in time?

strategy.explanation: Check the dates on each side of the blank.

candidates.remember: Use a time transition when a text moves forward chronologically.

candidates.stem: The student wants to explain why Franklin did not share the 1962 Nobel Prize. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 1952, Franklin and Raymond Gosling made Photo 51, an X-ray image of DNA.
choices.B: Wilkins showed Photo 51 to Watson in 1953 without Franklin's knowledge.
choices.C: The 1962 Nobel Prize for DNA's structure went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins.
choices.D: Franklin died in 1958, and Nobel Prizes are not awarded after death.

candidates.evidence: Nobel Prizes are not awarded after a person's death
candidates.explanation: Only choice D connects Franklin's death in 1958 with the rule against posthumous awards, which explains the outcome.

A.rationale: This describes her work but does not explain the prize outcome.

B.rationale: This describes how the image was used, not why she did not share the prize.

C.rationale: This states who won but not why Franklin was not included.

strategy.explanation: Find the notes that give a reason.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must accomplish the stated goal.

candidates.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?

choices.B: "Life is a broken-winged bird / That cannot fly."
choices.C: "Life is a barren field / Frozen with snow."

candidates.evidence: loses the ability to rise and move freely
candidates.explanation: A bird with a broken wing that cannot fly is unable to rise or move freely, matching the claim exactly.

A.rationale: This urges the reader to keep dreams but does not describe life without them.

C.rationale: This shows life without dreams as lifeless, but not as unable to rise or move.

D.rationale: This sets up the condition but says nothing about what life becomes.

hints: Which image shows an inability to rise?

strategy.explanation: Match each quotation to the specific claim.

candidates.remember: Choose the quotation that matches the claim's exact idea.

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (emphasizing significance to a community)
candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize why the 2019 discovery mattered to Africatown's residents. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2019, researchers confirmed that a wreck in the Mobile River was the Clotilda, which had been burned in 1860.
choices.B: For Africatown residents, including descendants of the ship's captives, the discovery confirmed a hidden history.
choices.C: The Clotilda arrived in Alabama in 1860, decades after the trade in enslaved people was outlawed in the United States.
choices.D: Africatown, a community near Mobile, Alabama, was founded by people who had been brought to the United States.

candidates.evidence: Descendants of those people still live in Africatown
candidates.explanation: Only choice B links the discovery to the residents, many of whom descend from the people the ship carried.

A.rationale: This states the discovery but not why it mattered to Africatown.

C.rationale: This gives background but does not mention the residents or the discovery.

D.rationale: This describes the community but not the discovery.

hints: Which choice connects the discovery to the residents?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice against the exact goal.

candidates.remember: A synthesis answer must address the goal's specific focus.

revision_history.reason: both blind solvers: "its captives" had no clear antecedent; "many descended" overstated the notes
revision_history.change: key reworded to "including descendants of the ship's captives"
